title: Hot Path, Cold Path, or Both? Routing a Streaming Workload
purpose: Decide, per streaming workload, whether events need Eventhouse's hot path, OneLake availability's cold path, or both — based on latency, retention, query pattern, and cost.
accessibleSummary: A decision tree that starts by asking what latency the workload actually needs. Sub-second alerting or live dashboards route to the Eventhouse hot path. Daily-freshness historical reporting or cross-domain joins route to the cold path via OneLake availability, and a workload needing both routes to both simultaneously since they're the same underlying table. A warning node covers the common mistake of keeping a hot event path running for a workload that only ever needed daily freshness, incurring streaming operational cost for no latency benefit a lakehouse or warehouse pipeline couldn't have delivered more cheaply.
longDescription: This is a decision tree for a question the streaming analytics pattern forces on every workload: which path, or both? The root question asks what latency the workload genuinely requires. A true operational need — an alert that must fire in seconds, or a live dashboard someone is watching in real time — routes to the Eventhouse hot path, where arrival-time indexing and in-place anomaly detection deliver that speed. A workload whose real requirement is historical trend analysis, cross-domain joins with warehouse or lakehouse dimensions, or reporting that only needs to be current within hours routes to the cold path via OneLake availability, which is not a separate pipeline but the same KQL table exposed as Delta. Because both paths share one underlying table, a workload that genuinely needs both — live alerting now and historical analysis later — gets both without extra ingestion work. A warning node names the cost trap of routing a purely daily-freshness workload through the hot path anyway, paying for an always-on Eventhouse and a caching policy tuned for query speed nobody needed, when a lakehouse or warehouse pipeline would have served the same daily requirement more cheaply.

nodes.label: What latency does this workload actually need?
nodes.summary: Root question: sub-second operational need, hours-scale historical need, or both.
nodes.detail: The first question in routing a streaming workload is not which Fabric item to use, but what latency the business requirement actually demands. Operational monitoring, anomaly investigation, and alerting genuinely need low latency; historical reporting and cross-domain joins do not, even though both can technically be served from the same Eventhouse-ingested data.
nodes.whyItMatters: Answering this honestly before building anything prevents the most common streaming cost trap: defaulting every workload onto the hot path because the data happens to already be streaming, regardless of what the business actually asked for.

inputs: The stated business requirement for this specific workload, not the data source's technical capability
Who consumes the result and how they use it (live monitoring vs periodic report)
processing: State the actual latency requirement in concrete terms (seconds, minutes, hours, daily)
Separate the requirement from the fact that the source happens to be a continuous event stream
outputs: A routed decision toward the hot path, the cold path, or both
drill.example: A safety-alert workload genuinely needs sub-minute detection and routes to the hot path; a weekly utilization trend report built from the same vehicle telemetry only needs the cold path, even though both read from the same Eventhouse.
controls: Write the latency requirement down in business terms before choosing an implementation path
failureModes: Routing every workload through the hot path because the data source is already streaming, rather than asking what each specific workload needs

nodes.label: Eventhouse hot path
nodes.summary: Sub-second, event-driven: live dashboards, anomaly detection, alerting conditions.
nodes.detail: Workloads with a genuine operational latency need route to the Eventhouse KQL database, which auto-organizes ingested records by arrival time for fast indexed queries and runs native anomaly detection in place against live time-series data, with no data copy or export required. This is also the path Activator watches to fire alerts and automated actions.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the path that actually delivers the sub-second responsiveness an operational requirement demands — the arrival-time indexing and in-place anomaly detection are specifically what make that speed possible without a separate real-time processing layer.

evidence.note: KQL database storage is split into a premium cache tier that holds the hot dataset governed by the caching policy, and a standard tier that holds the full retention window; configuring a shorter cache window reduces premium-tier spend without affecting total queryable history.

Eventhouses automatically organize ingested records by arrival time, enabling fast, indexed queries over structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale. Eventhouse includes native anomaly detection that evaluates live time-series and event datasets in place.

inputs: An event stream with a genuine sub-second-to-minutes latency requirement
processing: Route the eventstream to an Eventhouse KQL database
Size the caching policy's hot-cache window to cover exactly what live queries need
Connect Activator rules or a Real-Time Dashboard against the hot data
outputs: Live-queryable data supporting dashboards, alerting, and in-place anomaly detection
drill.example: A fleet-safety monitor needs to detect a stopped vehicle within a minute; it queries the Eventhouse hot cache directly rather than waiting on any batch or cold-path materialization.
controls: Caching policy window sized to the actual query need, not maximized by default
failureModes: Sizing the hot cache window larger than any live query actually needs, paying premium-tier cost for data nobody queries at low latency

nodes.label: OneLake availability (cold path)
nodes.summary: Hours-scale freshness: historical trends, cross-domain joins, daily/weekly reporting.
nodes.detail: Workloads whose real requirement is historical analysis, cross-domain joins with lakehouse or warehouse data, or reporting that's acceptable within hours route to OneLake availability — the same KQL table adaptively batched into Delta Parquet, queryable by lakehouse, warehouse, Spark, and Power BI Direct Lake with no data movement and no additional storage charge.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the cheaper, simpler path for anything that doesn't genuinely need sub-second freshness: no separate cold-path pipeline to build, since it's the same table the hot path already populated, just exposed as Delta.

evidence.note: Enabling OneLake availability exposes KQL table data in Delta Lake format, making it directly queryable by other Fabric engines — including Power BI Direct Lake mode, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks — without any data movement or copy, with no additional storage charge beyond standard OneLake storage.

An adaptive batching mechanism delays writes to OneLake until enough data accumulates to produce optimally-sized Parquet files. The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours; it can be lowered to as little as 5 minutes via the mirroring policy.

inputs: The same Eventhouse KQL table already receiving the event stream
processing: Enable OneLake availability at the table or database level
Adaptive batching writes Delta files on a delay tuned between 5 minutes and 3 hours
Downstream engines query the resulting Delta table like any other OneLake data
outputs: Historical, cross-engine-queryable data at whatever freshness the batching delay is tuned to
drill.example: A weekly fleet-utilization report joins the OneLake-available vehicle telemetry table with warehouse maintenance and contract dimensions, needing nothing faster than the default 3-hour batching delay.
controls: Mirroring policy delay setting, tuned to the actual freshness requirement rather than minimized by default
failureModes: Tuning the delay far below what the reporting cadence actually needs, producing many small files that degrade downstream query performance for no freshness benefit anyone uses

nodes.label: Both paths, same table
nodes.summary: A workload needing live alerting now and historical analysis later gets both with no extra ingestion.
nodes.detail: Because OneLake availability is a feature of the same KQL table rather than a separate ingestion pipeline, a workload that genuinely needs both live operational response and historical cross-domain analysis is served by enabling both the hot cache and OneLake availability on one table — no duplicated ingestion, no reconciliation between two copies.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the case that makes the hot/cold split a genuine architectural advantage rather than a compromise: the two latency profiles don't require choosing, or building and maintaining two separate pipelines that could drift apart.

inputs: A workload with both a genuine live-response requirement and a genuine historical/cross-domain requirement
processing: Keep the Eventhouse hot cache sized for the live query need
Enable OneLake availability on the same table for the historical/cross-engine need
Route Activator and dashboards against the hot cache; route reporting and joins against the OneLake Delta copy
outputs: One ingested table serving both a live alerting surface and a historical reporting surface
drill.example: A logistics team both alerts in real time when a vehicle goes offline (hot path) and builds a monthly on-time-delivery trend report joining the same telemetry with warehouse order data (cold path), from one Eventhouse table with both features enabled.
controls: Independent tuning of caching policy (hot) and mirroring policy delay (cold) on the same table
failureModes: Assuming enabling both paths doubles storage or ingestion cost, when OneLake availability adds no additional storage charge beyond standard OneLake storage

nodes.label: Trap: hot path for a daily-freshness workload
nodes.summary: Running an always-on hot path for a workload that only ever needed daily freshness wastes operational cost.
nodes.detail: Streaming adds cost and operational shape that batch workloads do not need. If the actual business requirement is daily freshness, a lakehouse or warehouse pipeline is usually a better fit than keeping a hot event path running — the hot path's premium cache tier and always-on Eventhouse capacity buy a latency benefit nobody asked for.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the most common streaming-analytics cost mistake: routing a workload onto the hot path by default because the source is already streaming, then paying for operational infrastructure that delivers no benefit over a much simpler scheduled pipeline.

evidence.note: Streaming adds cost and operational shape that batch workloads do not need; if the business requirement is daily freshness, a lakehouse or warehouse pipeline is usually a better fit than keeping a hot event path.

inputs: A workload with a stated daily (or slower) freshness requirement, currently routed through the Eventhouse hot path
processing: Re-examine the actual business requirement against the current implementation
Estimate the ongoing Eventhouse hot-cache cost versus an equivalent lakehouse/warehouse scheduled pipeline
Migrate the workload off the hot path if no genuine sub-daily need exists
outputs: Either a justified hot-path workload, or one correctly migrated to a cheaper scheduled pipeline
drill.example: A monthly compliance report was originally built on the Eventhouse hot path because the source data happened to be streaming; a review finds no consumer ever needed faster than daily freshness, and the workload is moved to a nightly lakehouse pipeline, eliminating the always-on premium cache cost.
controls: Periodic review of hot-path workloads against their actual stated freshness requirement, not just their data source's technical shape
failureModes: Nobody revisits the original routing decision after the workload ships, so the unnecessary cost persists indefinitely

edges.label: needs both live response and history
same table, hot cache already present
if the real need was only daily
migrate to a cheaper scheduled pipeline

walkthrough.title: 1. Ask what latency the workload needs, not what the source offers
walkthrough.explanation: The source being a continuous event stream doesn't mean every workload built on it needs hot-path latency.

walkthrough.title: 2. Hot path for genuine operational needs
walkthrough.explanation: Live dashboards, anomaly detection, and alerting conditions that must fire in seconds belong on the Eventhouse hot cache.

walkthrough.title: 3. Cold path for historical and cross-domain needs
walkthrough.explanation: OneLake availability serves hours-scale freshness at lower cost, since it's the same table exposed as Delta rather than a second pipeline.

walkthrough.title: 4. Both, when both are genuinely needed
walkthrough.explanation: A workload needing live response now and historical analysis later gets both from one table, with no duplicated ingestion.

walkthrough.title: 5. Warning: don't default to the hot path
walkthrough.explanation: A workload that only ever needed daily freshness pays ongoing hot-cache cost for a latency benefit nobody uses — the fix is migrating it to a scheduled pipeline.
